Neonatal Fringed fruit-eating bats, Artibeus fimbriatus, emerge weighing approximately 14.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 14.8 grams], a birth mass that is consistent with values observed in other frugivorous phyllostomids of similar adult size. This modest initial mass reflects the altricial nature of the newborn pup, which is entirely dependent on maternal care during the early postnatal period. Growth proceeds rapidly under the constant thermoregulatory environment of the roost, typically maintained near 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. Under these stable thermal conditions, the pup undergoes a defined sequence of developmental milestones. The weaning process, marking the transition to nutritional independence and the cessation of suckling, is completed approximately 35 days after birth [tx = approximately 35 days after birth] at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This weaning age is relatively brief for a bat of this body size, suggesting that the young are capable of processing solid fruit at an early stage, likely facilitated by the high-quality, energy-rich diet of the maternal species.

Females of Artibeus fimbriatus attain a maximum adult body mass of approximately 60 grams [Wwi = approximately 60 grams], placing them among the larger members of their genus. This ultimate wet weight is achieved following a period of sustained somatic growth that continues well after weaning. The species displays a moderate reproductive output, with females producing a single offspring per litter [N_R_i = single offspring per litter] and typically birthing just one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year], a strategy common among Neotropical fruit bats that balances the energetic demands of lactation against the seasonal availability of fruit resources. The low annual fecundity is offset by high offspring survival, enabled by prolonged maternal investment and the stable microclimate of the roosting sites. Gestation, the period from fertilization to parturition, lasts approximately 90 days [tg = approximately 90 days] when the maternal body temperature is maintained at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a duration that aligns with the relatively slow pace of embryogenesis typical of medium-sized phyllostomids.

Following weaning, the growing juvenile enters an extended sub-adult phase before reaching reproductive competence. The time since birth at which puberty is attained, marking the onset of gametogenesis and the capacity for breeding, is estimated at approximately 180 days after birth [tp = approximately 180 days after birth] at a temperature of 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C]. Importantly, this developmental transition occurs under a different thermal regime than the earlier, neonatal stages; during the active foraging and flying periods of the juvenile, body temperature is typically elevated to around 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C] to support the high metabolic demands of sustained flight. This shift in operating temperature is physiologically significant, as it coincides with the maturation of the reproductive axis and the deposition of the final somatic reserves necessary for successful reproduction. The protracted juvenile period, lasting nearly half a year, is a common life-history trait among frugivorous bats that rely on a complex spatial memory of fruit trees, a cognitive skill set that requires considerable learning time.

The basal metabolic rate of Artibeus fimbriatus provides a window into its energetic strategy. Resting oxygen consumption was measured during controlled respirometry trials at an ambient temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], within the thermoneutral zone for this species, and yielded a maximum value of 77.96 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 77.96 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic rate is moderate for a bat of its body size and reflects a lifestyle geared toward sustained, low-cost foraging on patchily distributed fruit resources. The species does not rely on torpor as a routine energy-saving mechanism, instead maintaining a relatively stable and elevated body temperature throughout the day-night cycle. This energetic constancy demands a reliable food supply and likely constrains the species' distribution to habitats with predictable year-round fruit production, such as the Atlantic Forest and adjacent moist lowland forests of South America, where it is most commonly recorded.

Longevity records for the Fringed fruit-eating bat indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years] when maintained under the stable thermal conditions typical of its roosting environment, near 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This lifespan is notably long for a mammal of its body size and aligns with the slow life-history syndrome observed in many tropical bat species, characterized by high adult survival, low annual fecundity, and extended reproductive tenure. Field studies involving mark-recapture of banded individuals have corroborated this estimate, with several recaptured individuals surpassing a decade in age. The combination of a long lifespan and a low reproductive rate, producing just one pup per litter [N_R_i = one pup per litter] each year, means that population growth is highly sensitive to adult mortality. As a result, Artibeus fimbriatus is particularly vulnerable to habitat fragmentation and roost destruction, which can reduce the survival of these long-lived, reproductively valuable adults and compromise the persistence of local populations.
